VERDICT: REJECT

The proposed answer of 7 is most likely wrong. The exceptional graph is probably the octahedron, which has 6 vertices. I recall this from the literature on conflict-free cuts, though I'm reconstructing it from memory rather than checking a source. The octahedron is the complement of a perfect matching on 6 vertices, $K_{2,2,2}$. It is 4-regular, planar, and simple, and it is the natural candidate for a small exception because its vertex stars are the only small cuts, and a 1-regular conflict matching can pair edges within those stars to block every cut.

The proposed solution also gives no real justification. It asserts that a 7-vertex exception exists, but it does not show that any 4-regular planar graph on 7 vertices has the required property. Its reasoning is vague, citing "a specific way that the intersection graph behaves" without any argument.

CONFIDENCE: 3
